lead.question: For all complex n-by-m matrices A and finite families of rectangles I_t×J_t covering every coordinate, must the operator 2-norm of A be at most the sum of the operator 2-norms of the restrictions to those rectangles?
lead.title: Quantum inspired matrix inequality
lead.decisive_test: Search cross-intersecting incidence families (rows and columns labelled by r-subsets of [2r−1]; rectangle t means both subsets contain t). For test matrices A depending only on intersection size the blocks lie in the Johnson association scheme. Maximize the uniform-vector Rayleigh quotient with each block norm ≤1 via rational linear inequalities in the orbit coefficients. Any strict violation certifies an explicit finite counterexample by exact matrix inequalities; no finite miss can prove the universal claim.
lead.blocker: The original poster identifies cancellation in the existing purported proof. The question is quantum-inspired matrix analysis, not an experimental prediction. May need other rectangle covers or a new norm-decomposition theorem. Ensure witnesses control complex singular values exactly before publication.
lead.previous_attempt: Uniform-vector objective over intersection-invariant matrices, r=2 through 18: exact maximum r, below the required 2r−1. A fresh attempt should address other eigenvectors or asymmetric covers.

review.statement: For every positive integer n, m and k, every A ∈ ℂ^{n×m}, and every family I_t ⊆ [n], J_t ⊆ [m] with 1 ≤ t ≤ k and ∀(i,j) ∈ [n]×[m] ∃t such that i ∈ I_t and j ∈ J_t, is ‖A‖₂ ≤ Σ_t ‖A|_{I_t,J_t}‖₂? The restriction is zero outside the rectangle, and ‖·‖₂ is the largest singular value. [Yu-Hsuan Huang’s original MathOverflow question](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/338936/quantum-inspired-matrix-inequality)
review.significance: The problem asks whether one can bound the spectral norm of a complex matrix by the total spectral norm of overlapping rectangular restrictions. Disjoint partitions satisfy the bound by the triangle inequality. With overlap, a proof has to account for the same entries appearing in several restrictions and for cancellation among complex entries.
review.settlement_test: A proof must establish the stated constant 1 for arbitrary finite rectangle covers and complex matrices. A refutation requires one finite matrix and a verified cover with a certified lower bound on the full spectral norm strictly exceeding the sum of certified upper bounds on the restriction norms.
review.aliases: The source title is “Quantum inspired matrix inequality.” Search variants included spectral-norm rectangle-cover inequality, operator-norm subadditivity over overlapping rectangular restrictions, and Schur-multiplier formulations. Huang reports deleting an earlier Mathematics Stack Exchange post before reposting on MathOverflow. I found no accessible copy of that post or later version of the same conjecture.
review.attempt: I used the original unformalized statement. The catalogue page and both attempted /agent.txt endpoints were inaccessible. No dedicated notebook interface was exposed, so I used an isolated JavaScript evaluation cell to check 171 coefficient identities in exact integer arithmetic for r=1 through 18. The argument below proves the inequality for the proposed incidence covers for every r and every complex matrix, removing the restriction to intersection-invariant matrices and uniform vectors. The search found no prior resolution of the arbitrary-cover statement. Dioniz’s MathOverflow answer attempts a stronger squared-norm inequality. Huang identified cancellation in that argument, which also equates a sum of suprema with a supremum of a sum. Hrubeš, Jukna, Kulikov and Pudlák’s On Convex Complexity Measures studies spectral norms under fractional partitions, where the weights give exact entrywise multiplicity one. [Dioniz’s answer and Huang’s comments](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/338936/quantum-inspired-matrix-inequality/338942) [On Convex Complexity Measures, §6](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2009/040/download/)
review.proof_or_witness: Proof for the proposed family. Index rows and columns by the r-subsets of [2r−1], and take rectangle t to consist of pairs (S,T) with t ∈ S∩T. The cover holds since |S∩T|≥1. Within rectangle t, multiply each entry by 1/|S∩T|. The weighted restrictions sum to A entrywise. To show that the weighting is contractive on each local block, delete t from both labels. The labels are now q-subsets of a 2q-element set, with q=r−1, and the multiplier is B_XY=1/(1+|X∩Y|). Complementing the column label turns this into C_XY=1/(1+q−|X∩Y|). For 0<z<1, the kernel z^(q−|X∩Y|) equals Σ_{L⊆X∩Y} z^(q−|L|)(1−z)^|L| by the binomial theorem. Each summand is a nonnegative multiple of the rank-one kernel 1_{L⊆X}1_{L⊆Y}. Integrating in z gives C, so C is positive semidefinite with diagonal one. Writing C as a Gram matrix of unit vectors u_X, the Schur product C∘M is V* (M⊗I) V for the isometry V e_X=e_X⊗u_X. Hence its operator norm is at most ‖M‖₂ over ℂ. Column permutation preserves the operator norm, giving the same contraction for B. The triangle inequality now proves the desired bound for these covers. Separately, the stronger squared-norm claim in Dioniz’s answer fails for the r=2 cover and A equal to the 3×3 all-ones matrix minus the identity. Its eigenvalues are 2, −1, −1, while all three local blocks have eigenvalues 1 and −1. The squared comparison is 4>3, and the original comparison is 2≤3.
review.remaining_obligation: An independent checker can verify the entrywise sum, the Gram kernel integral, and the column-permutation step directly. The universal claim remains open in this draft. Equal weighting by reciprocal multiplicity can fail to be contractive on a general cover. For example, a full 2×2 rectangle plus a singleton at (1,2) gives full-block weights [[1,1/2],[1,1]]. Applied entrywise to [[1,−1],[1,1]], the squared spectral norm rises from 2 to 9/4. The universal problem therefore still requires an argument that works for general covers or an exact strict counterexample.
